source.title: QUAIL: Quantization Aware Unlearning for Mitigating Misinformation in LLMs

page_placements.theme: Compression: quantization mechanism, precision changes and pruning

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table formatting and claims are inconsistent or unclear, noted under problems.
record.tranche_reason: It directly tests whether post-training quantization restores forgotten knowledge, using GA-GDR and QUAIL with MUSE and Twitter measures. The tested method and reported measures are not an exact reproduction of the listed original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for quantization attacks, targeted-knowledge measures, and retain-set utility. Bucket-overlap measurements and membership-inference leakage are recorded separately because they do not directly measure the knowledge-recovery behavior specified in versions A or D. The paper describes other quantization schemes in its setup, but the reported result tables do not separate outcomes by scheme.
record.test_reason: The study applies 4-bit post-training quantization to GA-GDR-unlearned LLaMA-2-7B on MUSE NEWS and reports forget-set M1/M2 before and after, which tests D and the quantization part of A. It also proposes QUAIL and reports its 4-bit M1/M2, which tests F. The listed originals are WMDP, Who's Harry Potter and Eight Methods. The quantization attack itself follows Zhang et al., not those originals, so this is T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that 4-bit quantization catastrophically restores knowledge forgotten by standard unlearning (recovery 'exceeding 80%'). They also say QUAIL's logit hinge loss preserves forgetting with competitive utility, and that it is hyperparameter-sensitive. Their own Table II does not show QUAIL lowering 4-bit M1/M2 relative to GA GDR. They also claim BOOKS results that are not reported.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses GA-GDR as a baseline and adds QUAIL, a logit-space quantization-aware hinge loss. This differs from the cited unlearning recipes in the claim’s original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity to α and γ; it says insufficient margins can fail to reduce overlap and overly large margins can reduce retain-set utility. Outcomes also differ between NEWS and Twitter and between full precision and 4-bit quantization.

fits_no_version.finding: Quantized bucket overlap between GA-GDR and reference weights reaches 100% global / 99.94% tensorwise at 4-bit. The mean weight change is 2.97e-5, below Δ/2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quantization maps small unlearning updates back into the reference model's weight buckets.

fits_no_version.finding: PrivLeak flips sign under 4-bit. QUAIL α=5,γ=8 at 4-bit has M3 −99.79, identical to the quantized target, contradicting the claimed leakage reduction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quantization returns membership-inference behaviour of unlearned models to that of the target.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The behavioral tables show only 16-bit and 4-bit values although the setup also describes 8-bit results; table outcomes are not separated by RTN, AWQ, and GPTQ. The Twitter table reports only M1. The paper's interpretation of PrivLeak sign changes is difficult to reconcile with its stated ideal value near zero, and some prose claims about QUAIL's selected NEWS results do not align clearly with the listed table values. The stated theoretical link from logit separation to weight-space boundary crossing is not established by the reported experiment. The text also mentions BOOKS in its summary and conclusion but provides no BOOKS results.
record.rows_left_out: Table II reports many additional M3 and M4 values and 16-bit values across the full set of GA GDR L1 hyperparameter combinations. The extract prioritizes the GA-GDR comparison, the selected α=5, γ=8 comparison, and all listed 4-bit M1/M2 hyperparameter results. Other per-configuration M3/M4 and 16-bit values are omitted because they are not direct measures of the targeted-knowledge recovery behavior.

untested.parts: General-ability benchmarks beyond retain-set KnowMem; attacks other than quantization.
All: no activation-direction ablation or behavioural access-vs-deletion test (weight bucket overlap only).
8-bit behavioural results; AWQ/GPTQ reported separately; models other than LLaMA-2-7B; unlearning methods beyond GA/GA-GDR (NPO mentioned but not reported); BOOKS.
QUAIL against fine-tuning, internal-edit and prompting attacks; 8-bit.

missing.what: Plain GA results: M1, M2 and M4 are all 0.0 at both 16-bit and 4-bit, showing no quantization recovery but full utility collapse.

16-bit M1/M2/M4 for hinge configs other than α=5,γ=8. Several configs have 16-bit M1 0.0, and α=5,γ=10 has all metrics 0.0, showing full recovery at 4-bit. rows_left_out declares these, but the D/F verdicts need them.
missing.locator: Table II, GA GDR L1 (16-bit) rows

record.verdict_notes: Several internal inconsistencies. The authors cite near-zero M3 for α=5,γ=8, but that is the 16-bit value; at 4-bit it equals the target's. Two configs share identical values, and the selected config's M4 nearly matches its M2. The Twitter 4-bit target is identical to 16-bit, and GA GDR never forgets on Twitter. The paper mentions 8-bit and AWQ/GPTQ but reports only 4-bit behavioural results by unstated scheme. There are no uncertainty estimates. It is a course-project preprint.

versions.untested_parts: General ability beyond the reported retain-set KnowMemr measure; attacks other than quantization.
No relearning fine-tuning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or subset examples is reported.
No activation-direction ablation or internal access-versus-deletion analysis is reported.
The reported behavioral results focus on 4-bit quantization; the paper does not provide separately reported knowledge-recovery results for each quantization method it describes.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context-information recovery test is reported.
QUAIL is evaluated against quantization, not against fine-tuning, internal edits, or prompting attacks.

statements.correction: Table II: plain GA M1 0.0 and M2 0.0 at 16-bit and 4-bit; M4 0.0 at both.
2601.15538, GA GDR baseline (no hinge loss): M2 24.35 at 16-bit, 49.54 at 4-bit; 4-bit target 54.45, 16-bit target 64.41. QUAIL configs' 4-bit M2 is 47.36-53.13.
statements.problem: Calls 49.54 'QUAIL's M2'. It is the 4-bit M2 of the GA GDR baseline without the hinge loss (r8), not of the QUAIL method.

statements.correction: QUAIL 4-bit M1 24.15-36.98 and M2 47.36-53.13. GA GDR 4-bit is 24.36 and 49.54, and the 4-bit target is 36.18 and 54.45. Every config is at, near (at most 2.2 points below) or above GA GDR, so none reduces 4-bit recovery meaningfully.
statements.problem: 'At or above GA GDR at 4 bits' contradicts the statement's own ranges. M1 24.15 (alpha 1, gamma 1) is below 24.36. M2 47.36 (alpha 1, gamma 1), 47.65 (alpha 5, gamma 10) and 47.86 (alpha 5, gamma 9) are below 49.54. The range endpoints 36.98 and 53.13 (alpha 20) come from rows r24-r29, which are not cited.

statements.correction: Remove 2601.15538 from this item, or state these facts. Alpha 5, gamma 8 at 16-bit: M1 26.13 and M2 54.68 against target 42.21 and 64.41, with M4 54.68 against target 53.91. At 4-bit: M1 35.03 and M2 49.66, against GA GDR's 24.36 and 49.54.
statements.problem: Cites r9 and r11 from this study but says nothing about it, and the study does not fit the point. QUAIL shows no resistance to 4-bit recovery. Its alpha 5, gamma 8 config keeps utility but forgets weakly at 16-bit.
